reviewer_gap: Three distinct accountability sub-requirements are absent from the submission: (1) No patient or clinician redress/grievance mechanism is documented — there is no process by which individuals adversely affected by an AI-assisted decision can raise a complaint, seek explanation, or obtain remedy, as required under the WHO accountability principle. (2) There is no description of how affected patients or groups can formally challenge or contest AI-assisted diagnostic decisions, leaving the WHO requirement for questioning and remedy mechanisms entirely unaddressed. (3) There are no training or qualification requirements defined for personnel who hold named accountability roles — WHO guidance explicitly requires that such roles be exercised by 'appropriately trained people', yet the submission contains no reference to competency standards, mandatory training programmes, or qualification criteria for those individuals.
reviewer_suggestion: Address all three gaps before the Certifier phase as follows: (1) Redress/Grievance Mechanism — Draft and ratify a formal Patient and Clinician Redress Policy that defines: a named complaints owner, intake channels (e.g., portal, written form), acknowledgement SLAs, escalation paths, and remediation outcomes. Map this policy to the relevant WHO accountability principle and reference it explicitly in the accountability section of the submission. (2) AI Decision Challenge Process — Document a structured procedure (SOP or workflow diagram) that enables patients or clinician groups to contest an AI-assisted diagnostic output. The procedure must specify who receives the challenge, how the AI reasoning is reviewed, what override authority exists, and how the outcome is communicated back to the challenger. Include at least one completed test-run or tabletop exercise as operational proof. (3) Training and Qualification Requirements — Define minimum competency standards for every named accountability role (e.g., required clinical informatics training, AI literacy certification, or equivalent qualification). Embed these requirements in role profiles or HR policy, establish a training register, and provide evidence that current role-holders meet the defined standards. All three artefacts should be cross-referenced within the main accountability policy to demonstrate cohesive coverage.
user_commitment: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

reviewer_gap: Four distinct deficiencies exist in the current scope documentation for this P1 / Documented Purpose and Scope control: (1) No version history or change-control log is present for the scope document itself, making it impossible to trace how scope boundaries have evolved or how changes are communicated to stakeholders. (2) There is no reference to a formal impact assessment process or third-party audit mechanism, which is required under WHO guidance Section 08.1 for systems at this assurance level. (3) The treatment of out-of-scope use enforcement is ambiguous — the phrase 'where feasible' is used without distinguishing which boundaries are enforced by technical controls versus policy-only controls, leaving a material gap in assurance. (4) Patient-facing and self-care use scenarios (relevant per WHO Section 04.1) are excluded from scope, but this exclusion is not documented as a deliberate, rationale-backed governance decision — it appears as an omission rather than an explicit choice.
reviewer_suggestion: Before the Certifier phase, take the following concrete steps: (1) VERSION CONTROL — Introduce a formal document version table (version number, date, author, summary of change, approver) into the scope document and back-populate at least the two most recent revisions. Establish and document a change-control SOP that specifies who must approve scope amendments and how changes are communicated to affected stakeholders. (2) IMPACT ASSESSMENT AND AUDIT REFERENCE — Add an explicit section to the scope document referencing the organisation's impact assessment process (e.g., a Data Protection Impact Assessment or AI Impact Assessment) and any scheduled or completed third-party audits, with pointers to the relevant artefacts. If no third-party audit has been conducted, document the planned timeline and responsible owner. (3) TECHNICAL VS. POLICY ENFORCEMENT — Produce a control mapping table that lists each out-of-scope use boundary and classifies it as either (a) technically enforced (with a reference to the specific technical control, configuration, or system constraint) or (b) policy-only (with a reference to the governing policy and any compensating controls). Remove or qualify the 'where feasible' language with this explicit mapping. (4) PATIENT-FACING EXCLUSION RATIONALE — Add a dedicated governance decision record to the scope document that explicitly states patient-facing and self-care scenarios are out of scope, provides the clinical, regulatory, or design rationale for this decision, names the accountable decision-maker, and records the date of the decision. Cross-reference WHO Section 04.1 to demonstrate awareness of the guidance.

reviewer_gap: The submission consists of a single sentence stating that a consultant radiologist must review and sign off all MediScan AI outputs before clinical action. This is wholly insufficient as a human oversight plan. Specifically absent are: (1) a real-time intervention mechanism allowing humans to interrupt or pause the AI mid-operation; (2) a defined process for handling radiologist disagreement with or override of AI outputs; (3) an escalation pathway or fallback procedure when the reviewing radiologist is unavailable; (4) documentation of radiologist training to critically evaluate MediScan AI outputs; (5) a mechanism for logging, auditing, and recording oversight decisions to satisfy post-release audit compliance (WHO Section 16.2); (6) transparency provisions informing patients and other stakeholders that AI is being used in their diagnosis; (7) coverage of edge cases such as urgent or emergency scenarios where the standard sign-off workflow may be bypassed; and (8) a process for monitoring and reviewing the ongoing effectiveness of the oversight regime. No supporting policy document, procedure, or evidence of implementation accompanies the submission.
reviewer_suggestion: Before the Certifier phase, the applicant must produce and submit a comprehensive Human Oversight Plan document addressing all of the following: (1) Real-time intervention — define the technical and procedural mechanism (e.g., a clearly labelled "Pause / Reject" control in the MediScan UI) by which a radiologist can halt or override the AI mid-operation, and document how this is surfaced in the clinical workflow; (2) Override and disagreement process — draft a written SOP specifying the steps a radiologist must follow when they disagree with an AI output, including how the disagreement is recorded, escalated if needed, and fed back for model improvement; (3) Escalation and fallback — define a tiered escalation pathway (e.g., on-call deputy radiologist, senior clinician, or safe-default hold) for situations where the primary reviewing radiologist is unavailable, with clear time-bound triggers; (4) Radiologist training programme — document a structured training curriculum covering MediScan AI capabilities, known limitations, confidence score interpretation, and critical evaluation techniques, including records of completion; (5) Audit logging — implement and document an automated logging mechanism that captures every oversight decision (review, approval, override, escalation) with timestamps and user IDs, aligned with WHO Section 16.2 requirements; (6) Patient and stakeholder transparency — draft a patient-facing disclosure statement and update consent forms to inform patients that AI is used in their diagnostic pathway, and document how this is communicated at the point of care; (7) Emergency/edge-case protocol — explicitly define the workflow for urgent or emergency scenarios, including any permitted derogations from the standard sign-off process, the conditions that trigger them, and the compensating controls applied; (8) Oversight effectiveness review — establish a periodic review cadence (e.g., quarterly) with defined metrics (override rate, escalation frequency, audit findings) and assign ownership for conducting and documenting these reviews.
user_commitment: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

reviewer_gap:
The submission addresses only one narrow incident type (false negatives) and provides only a single notification step, leaving the following entirely absent:

1. **Incident scope**: No coverage of cybersecurity breaches (e.g., prompt injection, data manipulation, ransomware), false positives causing clinical harm, data integrity failures, system outages, or other AI-specific incident categories.
2. **End-to-end response lifecycle**: No description of incident detection, logging, triage, containment, investigation, remediation, or post-incident review — only an initial notification is mentioned.
3. **Escalation timelines and SLAs**: No defined timeframes for internal escalation steps (e.g., maximum time to notify Clinical Governance Lead, CMO, or MHRA after incident detection).
4. **Regulatory obligations beyond UK MDR 2002**: No reference to serious risk/harm reporting obligations under EU AI Act Article 27 or other applicable frameworks (e.g., GDPR breach notification, NHS DSP Toolkit, WHO AI safety guidance).
5. **Detection and triage mechanisms**: No description of how incidents are identified, recorded, severity-classified, or queued for escalation.
6. **Patient safety communication**: No procedures for notifying affected patients, clinicians, or care teams in the event of a clinical harm incident.
7. **Cybersecurity-specific response**: No dedicated pathway for AI/cybersecurity threat scenarios as recommended in WHO guidance on AI in health.
8. **Roles and responsibilities**: No documented RACI or equivalent — only three notification recipients are named, with no defined ownership of response actions.
9. **Plan testing and exercising**: No evidence that the incident response plan has ever been tested, simulated, or drilled.

reviewer_gap: The submission addresses only a single training duration requirement for consultant radiologists and fails to demonstrate that oversight roles have been defined, assigned, or trained across the breadth expected for this control. Specifically: (1) no oversight role definitions exist — it is unclear who holds accountability for human oversight of the AI system beyond the radiologist reviewing outputs; (2) no evidence that roles such as clinical leads, AI governance officers, safety monitors, or multidisciplinary oversight representatives have been identified or scoped; (3) the content of the 4-hour training programme is entirely undescribed — there is no confirmation it covers oversight duties, escalation pathways, human-in-the-loop responsibilities, or bias/error recognition; (4) no ongoing or refresher training cadence is defined to maintain oversight competency over time; (5) no governance or accountability framework is documented to support structured human oversight; and (6) no alignment is demonstrated with regulatory expectations around cross-sectoral risk monitoring or multidisciplinary oversight as referenced in WHO guidance and UK AI regulation sources. The submission is limited to a single line of text (R1 only) with no corroborating policy, training materials, role descriptions, or organisational documentation.

DOCUMENT THE GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE: Create or reference an existing governance framework or accountability structure that situates these roles within the organisation's AI oversight model, aligned with UK AI regulatory expectations and WHO guidance on cross-sectoral risk monitoring. 3. reviewer_gap:
Four distinct deficiencies exist in the current submission for the Data Minimisation control (P4):

1. **Policy review cadence**: The data minimisation policy contains no explicit periodic review trigger (e.g., annual review cycle), version control history, or scheduled review dates, making it impossible to confirm the policy remains current and fit-for-purpose over time.

2. **EHR extract field enumeration**: Although 'Social history beyond what appears in the EHR extract' is excluded, the specific fields ingested from the EHR extract itself are not enumerated. It is therefore unverifiable whether the EHR extract is itself minimised to only necessary fields, leaving a potential over-collection risk unaddressed.

3. **Technical enforcement mechanisms**: There is no description of runtime controls — such as data masking, field-level access controls, schema allowlists, or pipeline validation rules — that would technically prevent non-necessary fields from being inadvertently ingested. The current posture relies entirely on policy intent rather than enforced technical guardrails.

4. **Staff training and awareness**: There is no reference to training programmes, awareness campaigns, or competency assessments that operationalise the data minimisation policy among staff who design, build, or operate data ingestion pipelines.
reviewer_suggestion:
Address each gap as follows before the Certifier phase:

1. **Policy review cadence** — Amend the data minimisation policy document to include: (a) an explicit review frequency (e.g., annual or triggered by material system change), (b) a version control table showing current and prior versions with dates and approvers, and (c) a named role responsible for initiating each review cycle. Provide the updated policy as evidence.

2. **EHR extract field enumeration** — Produce a data inventory or data-flow diagram that explicitly lists every field ingested from the EHR extract, maps each field to its documented clinical or operational necessity justification, and confirms that fields without a necessity justification are excluded. This should be reviewed and signed off by the Data Protection Officer or equivalent.

3. **Technical enforcement mechanisms** — Document and demonstrate the runtime controls that enforce minimisation at the ingestion layer. This should include: schema allowlists or field-level filters in the ingestion pipeline configuration, evidence of data masking or suppression rules for any fields conditionally present in source data, and results of integration or regression tests confirming that out-of-scope fields are rejected or masked. Provide configuration artefacts and test reports as evidence.

4. **Staff training and awareness** — Implement and document a training programme covering data minimisation obligations for all staff involved in data ingestion design and operations. Evidence should include training materials, a record of completion (names, dates, roles), and confirmation of the refresh cadence (e.g., on-boarding plus annual refresher).
user_commitment: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

reviewer_gap: The submission relies solely on a single lawful basis (UK GDPR Article 9(2)(h) — medical diagnosis) and references only parental consent for paediatric patients. It fails to: (1) identify lawful bases for all processing activities beyond primary diagnosis, including LMM/AI model training, secondary processing, administrative uses (e.g., drafting patient message responses), audit, and research; (2) demonstrate how meaningful informed consent is obtained from adult patients; (3) cite any additional Article 9(2) conditions (e.g., explicit consent under Article 9(2)(a)) applicable to non-diagnostic processing of special category health data; (4) describe any mechanism for recording, managing, or withdrawing consent; (5) address transparency obligations and how data subjects are informed of all processing purposes; (6) reference Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) or third-party audits as required under the applicable regulatory context; and (7) provide any supporting policy documentation, procedural artefacts, or implementation evidence — the submission is text-only (R1).
reviewer_suggestion: 1. LAWFUL BASIS MAPPING: Produce a comprehensive data processing register that maps every processing activity (diagnosis, model training, administrative use, audit, research, secondary processing) to a specific, documented lawful basis under UK GDPR Article 6 and a corresponding Article 9(2) condition. Where explicit consent (Article 9(2)(a)) is relied upon for non-diagnostic processing, this must be clearly stated and distinguished from Article 9(2)(h). 2. ADULT CONSENT MECHANISM: Draft and implement a formal informed consent procedure for adult patients that covers all processing purposes, is written in plain language, is freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, and is separate from any consent obtained for paediatric patients. 3. CONSENT MANAGEMENT: Implement and document a consent management system that records when consent was given, the version of the consent notice presented, and provides a clear, accessible mechanism for withdrawal. Produce SOPs governing this lifecycle. 4. TRANSPARENCY NOTICES: Create or update Privacy Notices / Fair Processing Notices to cover all identified processing purposes, referencing each lawful basis, data retention periods, and data subject rights, in compliance with UK GDPR Articles 13/14. 5. DPIA: Conduct and document a Data Protection Impact Assessment for high-risk processing activities (particularly AI/LMM model training on health data), including consultation with the Data Protection Officer (DPO) and, where required, the ICO. 6. SECONDARY PROCESSING: Explicitly address the compatibility test (UK GDPR Article 6(4)) or separate lawful basis for any further/secondary processing (model training, research, audit), referencing WHO guidance Section 07.3 requirements. 7. EVIDENCE PACKAGE: Submit all of the above as formal documented artefacts — policies, SOPs, consent forms, DPIA reports, and audit records — to replace the current text-only submission.
user_commitment: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

reviewer_gap: The submission consists of unverified text-only assertions (R1) with no supporting artefacts. Six substantive gaps are present: (1) Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) for UK-to-Sri Lanka and UK-to-AWS flows are referenced but their substance, risk findings, and applied mitigations are entirely undisclosed — it is impossible to determine whether residual risk was deemed acceptable; (2) there is no evidence that cross-border transfer controls have been mapped against WHO guidance on health data governance, which is directly relevant given the P4 privacy domain and clinical/patient data processed by an LMM/AI system; (3) data minimisation, purpose limitation, and health/clinical-data-specific safeguards applicable to cross-border transfers are wholly absent from the submission; (4) the AWS processor destination lacks specificity — no AWS region(s) are identified and no confirmation is provided of which UK GDPR Article 46 transfer mechanism (e.g., SCCs, adequacy decision, or binding corporate rules) applies to that route, nor whether the relevant AWS Data Processing Addendum is in scope; (5) there is no reference to an ongoing monitoring or periodic review cadence for the SCCs and TIAs, as required under a risk-based framework (e.g., aligned to the UK AI risk register approach described in the regulatory context); and (6) no documentary artefacts of any kind have been submitted to substantiate any of the above assertions.
reviewer_suggestion: Before the Certifier phase, take the following concrete steps: (1) Produce and submit redacted or summarised TIA reports for both the UK-to-Sri Lanka and UK-to-AWS transfer routes, explicitly documenting: the risk assessment methodology used, risks identified, a conclusion on acceptability of residual risk, and any supplementary technical or contractual mitigations applied (e.g., encryption in transit/at rest, pseudonymisation, access controls). (2) Prepare a mapping document or addendum to the TIAs demonstrating how each transfer control aligns with WHO guidance on health data governance for AI/ML systems processing patient or clinical data — cross-reference specific WHO principles (e.g., data sovereignty, purpose limitation, accountability) against implemented controls. (3) Explicitly document data minimisation and purpose limitation measures applied to health/clinical data prior to cross-border transfer, and identify any additional safeguards specific to sensitive health data categories under UK GDPR Article 9. (4) For the AWS transfer route, specify the exact AWS region(s) involved, confirm the applicable UK GDPR Article 46 transfer mechanism in use (e.g., UK International Data Transfer Agreement / Addendum to EU SCCs), and attach or reference the executed AWS Data Processing Addendum. (5) Establish and document a formal review cadence (e.g., annual or triggered by material change) for all SCCs and TIAs, and record this within the organisation's AI risk register or data governance framework, with a named owner and next review date. (6) Submit all of the above as referenced, versioned documentary artefacts — not text assertions — so that each claim can be independently verified by the Certifier.

reviewer_gap: The submission identifies only two protected characteristic groups (South Asian patients and paediatric patients under 12) with no consideration of other legally and ethically relevant characteristics such as sex/gender, race beyond South Asian populations, disability status, socioeconomic status, or age groups outside the paediatric under-12 bracket (e.g., elderly patients). There is no documented systematic methodology underpinning how these characteristics were selected (e.g., bias audit, dataset demographic analysis, or structured fairness assessment). The accuracy disparity risk is asserted qualitatively but is not quantified or evidenced with measurement data. The stated mitigation measures (supplementary fine-tuning and mandatory senior radiologist review) lack detail on how their effectiveness will be monitored, validated, or reviewed over time. Finally, there is no documented consideration of how cybersecurity vulnerabilities (per WHO Section 05.6) or patient-centred use contexts (per Section 04.1) may intersect with or compound fairness risks for the identified or unidentified groups.
reviewer_suggestion: 1. EXPAND PROTECTED CHARACTERISTICS COVERAGE: Conduct and document a structured fairness scoping exercise that systematically evaluates all relevant protected characteristics — including sex/gender, race (beyond South Asian), disability status, socioeconomic status, and age groups such as elderly patients — against the training and validation dataset demographics. Produce a written rationale for inclusion or exclusion of each characteristic. 2. DOCUMENT THE IDENTIFICATION METHODOLOGY: Formalise the process used to identify protected characteristics into a reproducible methodology (e.g., bias audit protocol, dataset demographic analysis report, or structured fairness assessment framework). This should reference recognised standards or guidance (e.g., WHO AI ethics principles, Equality Act 2010 protected characteristics, or equivalent). 3. QUANTIFY ACCURACY DISPARITIES: Run and document subgroup performance analyses across all identified protected characteristic groups, reporting disaggregated metrics (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC) with statistical confidence intervals. Clearly evidence the degree of disparity rather than asserting it. 4. DETAIL AND OPERATIONALISE MITIGATION MONITORING: Expand the mitigation section to include a monitoring and review plan — specifying KPIs for fine-tuning effectiveness, review cadence for senior radiologist oversight, escalation thresholds, and a defined re-evaluation trigger (e.g., post-deployment performance drift). 5. ADDRESS INTERSECTING RISK DOMAINS: Document explicitly how cybersecurity vulnerabilities (WHO Section 05.6) and patient-centred use contexts (Section 04.1) may interact with fairness risks — for example, whether adversarial inputs or access inequities could disproportionately affect already-disadvantaged groups — and incorporate these considerations into the risk register.

reviewer_gap: The submission describes NHS smart card SSO with RBAC and audit logging, but four material gaps remain: (1) no controls or procedures governing third-party/vendor access to the AI system or its underlying data, leaving external threat vectors (including prompt injection pathways) unaddressed; (2) no periodic access review or recertification process to validate that RBAC assignments remain appropriate over time; (3) no description of how access controls are enforced specifically at the AI model/API layer, as distinct from EHR or record-level controls — it is unclear whether API authentication, authorisation scopes, rate limiting, or token management exist; and (4) no controls addressing unauthorised disclosure risks at the point of data submission to the LLM itself, such as data minimisation strategies or de-identification/pseudonymisation applied before AI processing.
reviewer_suggestion: 1. THIRD-PARTY/VENDOR ACCESS: Document and implement a formal vendor access control policy covering onboarding, least-privilege provisioning, MFA enforcement, session monitoring, and offboarding for any third party with access to the AI system or its data. Map this to WHO and DSPT guidance on external threat vectors and prompt injection risks. Provide the policy and evidence of its application to current vendors. 2. PERIODIC ACCESS REVIEW: Establish and evidence a recertification schedule (e.g., quarterly for privileged roles, semi-annually for standard roles) for all RBAC assignments. Provide records of at least one completed review cycle, including who reviewed, what was changed or confirmed, and sign-off by an accountable owner. 3. AI MODEL/API LAYER CONTROLS: Separately document the access control architecture at the AI/API layer, covering API key or OAuth token management, role-based API authorisation scopes, rate limiting, and any network-layer restrictions (e.g., IP allowlisting, private endpoints). Provide configuration evidence and a test report confirming enforcement. 4. DATA MINIMISATION BEFORE AI PROCESSING: Define and implement a data minimisation or de-identification procedure applied to patient data before it is submitted to the LLM. Document the fields suppressed or pseudonymised, the technical mechanism enforcing this, and any residual disclosure risk assessment. Provide the SOP and technical configuration as evidence.

reviewer_gap:
The submission demonstrates only a minimal baseline (checksum verification at acquisition and a 7-day patch evaluation window) but leaves six substantive gaps unaddressed:

1. **Model Bill of Materials (MBOM):** No provenance documentation exists covering upstream training data lineage, embedded third-party components, fine-tuning dependencies, or the full supply chain of the LLaMA Vision model. Checksum verification confirms file integrity at download but does not constitute supply chain transparency.

2. **Post-acquisition integrity and tamper controls:** There is no evidence of runtime integrity checks, cryptographic signing of model artefacts, secure storage controls (e.g., access-controlled model registries), or audit logging of who accessed or modified model weights/configs after acquisition.

3. **Prompt injection mitigations:** Prompt injection — explicitly flagged in WHO cybersecurity guidance for AI-enabled medical devices — is entirely unaddressed. No input validation, output sanitisation, sandboxing, or adversarial prompt testing is described.

4. **Patch-induced behavioural/clinical regression testing:** The 7-day patch evaluation window is stated but the *content* of that evaluation is undefined. There is no described process for assessing whether a security patch alters model behaviour, output distributions, or clinical performance prior to re-deployment.

5. **Sensitive data input controls:** No controls are described for data fed into the model at inference time (e.g., de-identification, access restrictions, data minimisation, logging of inputs/outputs), leaving unauthorised disclosure and secondary-use risks unmitigated per WHO Section 05.6.

6. **AI supply chain governance framework:** The submission is scoped to a single model instance. No policy or procedural framework exists for governing future model acquisitions, third-party provider model evaluations, or AI value chain partner assessments as required by WHO Section 06.1.
user_commitment: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

reviewer_gap: The submission reduces societal benefit to a single quantitative detection target (15% improvement) and a vague reference to quarterly equity monitoring, leaving four substantive dimensions entirely unaddressed: (1) No affordability mechanisms, language accessibility provisions, or digital-divide mitigation strategies are described for underserved or resource-poor populations in Sri Lanka or equivalent UK cohorts — monitoring alone does not constitute a benefit-realisation plan. (2) Patient-centred and self-care dimensions of societal benefit are absent — there is no discussion of patient empowerment, health literacy improvement, or clinician burden reduction, all of which are recognised societal benefit indicators under the applicable regulatory context. (3) The derivation and validation of the intended benefit claim is not evidenced — there is no reference to a clinical evidence base, national health priority alignment (e.g., NHS Long Term Plan, Sri Lanka National Cancer Control Programme), or stakeholder/community consultation that substantiates the 15% target as meaningful and achievable. (4) The equity monitoring commitment is undefined — no metrics, no measurement methodology, no threshold criteria, and no remediation or escalation actions that would be triggered by inequitable outcomes are specified, rendering the commitment unverifiable and unenforceable.
reviewer_suggestion: 1. BENEFIT REALISATION FOR UNDERSERVED POPULATIONS: Produce a written access and equity plan that explicitly describes affordability mechanisms (e.g., tiered pricing, public-sector licensing), multilingual interface provisions or translation pathways, and concrete steps to address infrastructure/digital-divide barriers in Sri Lanka and low-resource UK settings. This should reference specific population segments and deployment contexts. 2. PATIENT-CENTRED BENEFIT NARRATIVE: Expand the societal benefit statement to include patient-facing outcomes — document how the system supports patient empowerment (e.g., earlier informed decision-making), reduces clinician administrative or diagnostic burden, and/or improves health literacy. Reference relevant regulatory guidance (e.g., MHRA AI framework, Sri Lanka NMRA expectations) that recognises these as valid benefit dimensions. 3. BENEFIT DERIVATION AND VALIDATION: Provide a traceable evidence base for the 15% detection improvement claim — cite peer-reviewed clinical literature, reference alignment with national cancer strategies in both jurisdictions, and document any stakeholder or patient/community consultation conducted. If the target was set internally, provide the methodology and assumptions used. 4. EQUITY MONITORING FRAMEWORK: Define the equity monitoring programme in full: specify the metrics to be tracked (e.g., sensitivity/specificity disaggregated by demographic group, access rates by region/income), the data collection and analysis methodology, the frequency and governance of review, the threshold values that constitute an inequitable outcome, and the documented remediation or escalation actions that will be triggered. Formalise this as a standing operational procedure.
user_commitment: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.
